candidates.label: Galatia (region and Roman province, label point)
candidates.support: Galatia was, per Wikidata, the highland area of central Asia Minor; Celtic (Gaulish) migrants had migrated to Asia Minor by 278 BC, and the region was organized as a Roman province in 25 BC (per bib:zondervan-who-were-galatians). The label point is Wikidata's coordinate for the region; Pleiades' 'Galatia' province/region label (a separate entity from the late Roman 'Galatia I' record) is about 90 km away, a reasonable margin for a region label.

summary.text: Galatia was both an ethnic homeland of Celtic settlers in the highlands of central Asia Minor and, from 25 BC, a much larger Roman province of the same name. Celtic migrants, whom the Greeks and Romans called Galatians, had crossed into Asia Minor by 278 BC and settled around the headwaters of the Sangarios river and the middle course of the Halys. The Roman province, formed when Rome annexed the client kingdom in 25 BC, reached far south of this Celtic homeland to take in parts of Phrygia, Pisidia, and Lycaonia, including the cities of Antioch in Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe.

history.text: Paul's letter to the Galatians is addressed to "the assemblies of Galatia," but which congregations he meant has long been debated. The "North Galatian" view holds that he wrote to ethnic-Galatian congregations in the province's northern, Celtic-settled region; the "South Galatian" view holds that he wrote to the congregations in the province's southern cities, which he reached on his first missionary journey. This map favors neither view. Acts twice describes Paul traveling through the region of Galatia and nearby Phrygia, and in 1 Corinthians he mentions a collection organized among "the assemblies of Galatia."

The Roman province of Galatia was formed in 25 BC and governed from the city of Ancyra; in its larger first-century extent it also included Pisidia and Lycaonia, until the emperor Vespasian detached most of Pisidia in AD 74. The letter of 1 Peter is addressed to believers scattered across Galatia and four neighboring regions: Pontus, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia.
Galatia's former territory lies today within Türkiye, across the high country of the Anatolian plateau.

politicalHistory.note: Includes Pisidia, Lycaonia (the western part) and Paphlagonia, which had already joined the province of Galatia (Pisidia and Lycaonia in 25 BC on King Amyntas's death; Paphlagonia in 6 BC) before 4 BC. Vespasian detached most of Pisidia to the new province of Lycia and Pamphylia in AD 74; no source describing exactly where that internal line ran was found, so this area is kept whole rather than guessing at a split. Galatia and Cappadocia may have shared one governor from about AD 69 (see the Cappadocia area's own note), though no ancient source states a merger outright, so they stay two areas with their own holders.
